title: RAW UNREVIEWED: Pliny rue and hemlock: a reported poison is countered and collectors receive a different application
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. Rue juice in a large dose is called poisonous; hemlock juice is said to oppose it and to protect the hands and face of rue collectors. Nearby rue preparations are themselves antidotal. Preserve material, dose, application site and object of protection instead of giving either plant one fixed good/bad meaning.

source.work: Pliny, Natural History, Book XX, Bostock/Riley VolumeIV
source.span: Chapter51 Rue: eighty-four remedies, first three paragraphs, from cultivated/wild kinds through antidotal preparations
source.layer: Historical primary work in an explicitly named translation; source content inspected, no medieval Voynich ownership implied

differentiating_relation: RUE_JUICE at HIGH_DOSE has a harmful role; HEMLOCK_JUICE counters that harm, with an explicit topical application to COLLECTOR_HANDS_FACE during RUE_GATHERING. A separate RUE_LEAF_WINE preparation has an antidotal role. These are directed and scoped relations, not mutual universal cancellation.
complete_source_account: The opening differentiates cultivated and wild rue and describes juice preparation.
A large juice dose is harmful; the Macedonian variety is singled out; hemlock juice is described as opposing its effects and as applied to collectors’ hands and faces.
The next paragraph places rue in antidotes and gives bruised leaves in wine as a separately prepared antidotal use.
known_counterexplanation: A fixed plant-goodness lexicon makes rue always helpful or hemlock always harmful. A single-route account conflates topical collector protection with swallowing an antidote. A reciprocal-cancellation account invents a claim that rue counters hemlock, which these selected paragraphs do not state.
